Spark Theory: why it exists, how it runs, where it fits

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 0 · Class notes

0.1 The problem: data that no longer fits on one machine

Scale up (one bigger machine) Scale out (many ordinary machines)
How More RAM, more cores, faster disk Add machines to a cluster
Limit The biggest machine you can buy Practically none
Cost Rises steeply at the high end Grows roughly in line with size
Failure One machine down = everything down A machine down = its work is redone elsewhere
Examples pandas, a single PostgreSQL server Hadoop MapReduce, Spark

A laptop holds a few GB in memory; a company's click logs, orders and sensor data reach terabytes per day. Past a point no single machine can store or process that in time.

Spark's answer is to split the data into pieces, process the pieces in parallel on many machines, and combine the results — while hiding most of that complexity behind a DataFrame API that looks like pandas and SQL.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 0 · Class notes

0.2 From MapReduce to Spark

Year Milestone
2004 Google publishes the MapReduce paper: map over pieces, shuffle by key, reduce
2006 Hadoop brings MapReduce and HDFS (distributed storage) to everyone
2009 Spark starts at UC Berkeley's AMPLab: keep data in memory between steps
2014 Spark becomes a top-level Apache project; Spark 1.0
2016 Spark 2.0: SparkSession, DataFrames everywhere, Structured Streaming
2020 Spark 3.0: Adaptive Query Execution, faster Python (Arrow)
2025 Spark 4.0: ANSI SQL mode by default, Spark Connect, Python data sources

MapReduce wrote every intermediate result to disk, so a 10-step job read and wrote the data 10 times. Iterative work (machine learning, graph algorithms, interactive analysis) was painfully slow.

Spark keeps intermediate data in memory and plans the whole chain of steps before running it. These notes use Spark 4.2.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 0 · Class notes

0.3 Why Spark is fast

Idea What it means Where you will see it
Parallelism Data is split into partitions; each core works on one Chapter 1, Chapter 10
In-memory processing Steps pass data in memory instead of through disk cache(), pipelined stages
Lazy evaluation Nothing runs until you ask for a result, so Spark sees the whole plan Chapter 1
Query optimiser (Catalyst) Rewrites your plan: pushes filters down, prunes columns, picks join strategies explain() everywhere
Code generation (Tungsten) Turns a chain of steps into compact Java bytecode *(1) in plans
Columnar files Reads only the columns and row groups a query needs Parquet, Delta — Chapter 3, Chapter 12
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 0 · Class notes

0.4 One engine, many workloads

Library Use it for Chapter
Spark SQL / DataFrames Batch ETL, reporting, ad-hoc analysis — the core of this course 1–11
Structured Streaming Continuous pipelines from Kafka, files, event hubs 13
MLlib Distributed feature engineering and model training 16
pandas API on Spark pandas syntax on big data 11
Spark Connect Thin clients that talk to a remote Spark cluster —

The same DataFrame, the same optimiser and the same cluster serve all of them. You can read a stream, join it with a batch table, score it with a model and write the result — in one program and one language.

Spark has APIs in Python, SQL, Scala, Java and R. PySpark is the Python API; most of the real work still runs inside Spark's JVM engine.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 0 · Class notes

0.5 The architecture: driver, executors, cluster manager

Part What it does On your laptop (local[4])
Driver Runs your program, builds the plan, splits it into tasks, collects results Your Python process + a JVM
Executors Processes on worker machines that run tasks and hold cached data Threads inside the same JVM
Cluster manager Hands out machines, cores and memory Not needed
Task One unit of work on one partition of data One thread

On a real cluster the cluster manager is YARN, Kubernetes or Spark Standalone, and each executor is a separate JVM on a worker machine. On Databricks, EMR or Dataproc the platform runs the cluster manager for you.

The driver never touches the data itself unless you bring it back with collect() or toPandas() — then the whole result must fit in the driver's memory.

PySpark is a thin Python layer: your DataFrame calls are sent to the JVM through Py4J, and the JVM does the real work. That is why built-in functions are fast and Python UDFs are slow (Chapter 11).
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 0 · Class notes

0.6 Partitions, tasks and shuffles

Term Meaning
Partition A chunk of the rows. A 10 GB file might become 80 partitions of 128 MB
Task Processing one partition through a sequence of steps; one core runs one task at a time
Narrow transformation Each output partition depends on one input partition: filter, select, withColumn
Wide transformation Rows must move between machines so equal keys meet: groupBy, join, orderBy, distinct
Shuffle That movement: data is written, sent over the network and read again — the expensive part
Stage A run of narrow steps between two shuffles
Job All the stages needed to answer one action

Most of Spark performance work is about shuffles: avoiding unnecessary ones, making them smaller, and keeping their partitions evenly sized. Chapter 10 does this with real plans.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 0 · Class notes

0.7 Lazy evaluation: transformations plan, actions run

You write What Spark does
df = spark.read.parquet(...) Reads only the schema and file list
df2 = df.filter(...).select(...) Adds steps to a plan — no data is read
df3 = df2.groupBy(...).agg(...) Adds more steps — still nothing runs
df3.show() / count() / write Action: Catalyst optimises the whole plan, splits it into stages and tasks, and runs it

Because nothing runs until the action, Spark can, for example, read only the 2 columns used out of 50, and apply a filter written last as early as the file scan. You write the logic in the order that is clear to you; Spark reorders it for speed.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 0 · Class notes

0.8 RDD, DataFrame, Dataset

API What it is Optimised by Catalyst? In PySpark
RDD A distributed collection of objects, transformed with functions (map, filter, reduceByKey) No — functions are opaque Available, legacy; avoid for new code
DataFrame A distributed table with named, typed columns Yes The API you will use
Dataset A typed DataFrame bound to a class Yes Scala/Java only

A DataFrame is like a pandas DataFrame or a SQL table, but split across machines and evaluated lazily. Everything in Chapters 1–16 uses DataFrames (and SQL, which compiles to the same plans).

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 0 · Class notes

0.9 Spark, pandas and PostgreSQL side by side

pandas PostgreSQL Spark
Runs on One machine, in memory One server (plus replicas) Many machines
Data size Up to RAM Up to one server's disk Terabytes to petabytes
Evaluation Eager — every line runs now Per query Lazy — runs on an action
Storage None of its own Its own tables Files you own: Parquet, Delta, CSV
Transactions No Full ACID, row-level Via table formats such as Delta Lake
Best for Small analysis, plotting Applications (OLTP), many small reads/writes Batch ETL, big aggregations, streaming, ML features

These tools complement each other: an application writes orders to PostgreSQL, Spark processes the history of all orders into analytics tables, and an analyst pulls a small aggregated result into pandas to plot it.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 0 · Class notes

0.10 Where Spark fits in a data platform

Layer Typical tools Spark's role
Sources App databases (PostgreSQL), event streams (Kafka), files, APIs Reads from all of them
Ingestion Kafka, Fivetran/Airbyte, file drops, CDC Structured Streaming or batch reads
Storage (the lake / lakehouse) S3, ADLS, GCS with Parquet, Delta Lake, Iceberg Writes and maintains the tables
Processing Spark, dbt, Flink Cleans, joins and aggregates
Orchestration Airflow, Databricks Workflows Is the job being scheduled
Serving BI tools (Power BI, Tableau), ML models, APIs Produces the tables they read

Spark is the processing engine in the middle. It does not store data itself — it reads files and tables from cheap object storage and writes new ones back. That separation of storage and compute is why a lake can hold petabytes and still scale its processing up and down on demand.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 0 · Class notes

0.11 Preview: the medallion architecture (Bronze → Silver → Gold)

Layer Holds Built in this course
Bronze — raw Data exactly as it arrived, plus load metadata; append-only Chapter 3: reading and landing files
Silver — clean Typed, deduplicated, validated, conformed data Chapter 4: built-in functions for cleaning
Gold — business Aggregated tables for reports, dashboards and ML Chapter 5: aggregations
All three, properly Delta tables with MERGE, SCD2 and incremental loads Chapter 12
End to end The ShopKart pipeline, Bronze → Silver → Gold Chapter 15 capstone

Most lakehouses organise tables in these three layers. Keeping the raw Bronze copy means you can always rebuild Silver and Gold when a cleaning rule changes or a bug is found — nothing upstream has to be re-sent.

Watch for the layer labels in Chapters 3, 4 and 5: each one ends by writing its layer.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 0 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 0

  1. Spark scales out: data is split into partitions processed in parallel across a cluster.
  2. It improved on MapReduce by keeping data in memory and optimising the whole plan before running it.
  3. Driver plans and coordinates; executors run tasks; the cluster manager (YARN, Kubernetes, Standalone) provides the machines.
  4. Partition → task → stage → job. Shuffles (wide transformations) split stages and dominate cost.
  5. Lazy evaluation: transformations build a plan, actions (show, count, collect, write) run it.
  6. Use DataFrames (and SQL) in PySpark; RDDs are legacy.
  7. Spark is the processing layer of a lakehouse: it reads and writes files on object storage, it is not a database.
  8. Medallion: Bronze (raw) → Silver (clean) → Gold (business-ready).
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 0 · MCQ

Concept

What is the main reason Spark is faster than classic Hadoop MapReduce for multi-step jobs?

B. MapReduce writes intermediate results to disk between steps; Spark pipelines steps in memory and plans the whole job first.

Chapter 1 · Class notes

1.0 Start Spark and build the first DataFrame (continued)

Explanation

SparkSession is the single entry point to Spark. builder ... getOrCreate() returns the running session if one exists, otherwise it starts one. local[4] means "no cluster — use 4 cores of this machine".

createDataFrame turns a Python list of tuples into a distributed DataFrame. The second argument names the columns; Spark infers the types from the values.

F is the conventional alias for pyspark.sql.functions — almost every column function lives there.

Nothing is computed yet. Creating a DataFrame only records what the data is; Spark does work only when you ask for a result.

1.1 Which Spark did getOrCreate() give you?

Explanation

spark.version is the Spark release. master shows where the work runs: local[4] = 4 worker threads on this machine (on a cluster you would see yarn, k8s://… or spark://…).

defaultParallelism is how many tasks Spark runs at the same time by default — here one per core.

1.4 Ask for the toppers — and notice that nothing runs (continued)

4Explanation

filter is a transformation. It returns a new DataFrame immediately, but no rows were read and no job started — print(toppers) shows only the schema.

This is lazy evaluation: Spark keeps adding steps to a plan and waits until an action needs a result. That lets it optimise the whole chain before running anything.

Transformations return a DataFrame. Actions return a value (a number, a list, printed rows) — that is the quickest way to tell them apart.

Chapter 1 · Class notes

1.7 How is the data split? (partitions) (continued)

Explanation

A DataFrame is split into partitions — chunks of rows. One task processes one partition, so the number of partitions is the maximum parallelism of a stage.

spark.range(n) builds a DataFrame of numbers without any input file; it is the quickest way to make big test data.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 1 · Class notes

1.8 Which partition does each row live in?

Explanation

repartition(4) reshuffles the rows into 4 partitions, and spark_partition_id() tags each row with the partition it sits in.

The counts are roughly equal: repartition spreads rows round-robin. Uneven partitions (skew) are a major cause of slow jobs — Chapter 10 shows how to spot and fix them.

2Question

1.10 A wide transformation adds a shuffle (continued)

4Explanation

groupBy needs all rows of one branch on the same executor, so Spark must move data across the network. That move is the Exchange hashpartitioning(branch, …) line — a shuffle.

Spark aggregates twice: a partial HashAggregate before the shuffle (fewer rows to send) and a final one after it. Every Exchange splits the job into a new stage. The 200 is spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, the default number of partitions after a shuffle; AdaptiveSparkPlan means Adaptive Query Execution may shrink it at run time.

Narrow transformations (filter, select, withColumn) keep each partition where it is. Wide ones (groupBy, join, orderBy, distinct, repartition) shuffle. Count the Exchange lines to count the shuffles.
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 1 · Class notes

1.11 The same thing with the RDD API (for context)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 1 · Class notes

1.11 The same thing with the RDD API (for context) (continued)

Explanation

The RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset) is Spark's original low-level API: a distributed collection of Python objects transformed with lambdas. The classic word count is flatMap → map → reduceByKey.

In PySpark you should use DataFrames instead: Spark cannot look inside a Python lambda to optimise it, and every row must be moved between the JVM and Python. Learn the RDD only to read old code and to understand the model.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

1.12 Move between pandas and Spark (continued)

4Explanation

toPandas() is an action that collects the rows to the driver as a pandas DataFrame — handy for plotting a small, already-aggregated result. createDataFrame(pdf) goes the other way.

Chapter 1 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 1

  1. SparkSession is the entry point. SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate() returns the running session or starts one.
  2. Driver vs executors: your Python program is the driver; it plans the job. Executors run tasks on partitions of the data.

  3. Transformations are lazy (filter, select, withColumn, groupBy, join). Actions run the job (show, count, collect, take, first, write, toPandas).

    Transformation (returns a DataFrame) Action (returns a result)
    filter, where, select, withColumn show, count
    groupBy().agg(), join, orderBy collect, take, first
    distinct, repartition, union toPandas, write…save

  4. Narrow transformations keep data in place; wide ones (groupBy, join, orderBy, distinct) cause a shuffle — an Exchange in the plan and a new stage.

  5. One partition = one task. Partitions decide parallelism; uneven partitions (skew) make one task slow.
  6. collect() brings everything to the driver — use show(), take(n) or write to files for big data.
  7. Read plans with explain() bottom-up. Count Exchange lines to count shuffles.
  8. Use DataFrames, not RDDs, in PySpark: the optimiser can see DataFrame expressions but not Python lambdas.
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 1 · Deep dive

Job → stages → tasks

Level Created by Example
Job Every action count() = 1 job
Stage Splitting the job at each shuffle (Exchange) groupBy().count() = 2 stages
Task One per partition in a stage 4 partitions = 4 tasks

Inside a stage, Spark pipelines all narrow steps over a partition without writing anything in between. At a stage boundary the map side writes shuffle files and the next stage reads them over the network.

Open the Spark UI at <code>http://localhost:4040</code> while your session runs to see every job, stage and task.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 1 · Deep dive

Lineage: how Spark survives a lost executor

Explanation

Spark does not copy data for safety. It remembers the lineage — the chain of steps that produced each partition. If an executor dies, Spark re-runs those steps for just the lost partitions.

The map and filter lambdas were fused into one PythonRDD step, built on the ParallelCollectionRDD that holds the original numbers; (2) is the partition count. That is the "Resilient" in RDD, and it is why transformations must be deterministic.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 1 · MCQ

Concept

How many stages does students.groupBy("branch").count().show() need?

B. One shuffle (the Exchange for groupBy) splits the job into 2 stages: partial aggregation before the shuffle, final aggregation after it.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 1 · MCQ

Concept

Why should PySpark code prefer DataFrames over RDDs?

B. Catalyst optimises DataFrame plans and Tungsten runs them in the JVM. RDD lambdas are opaque Python functions, so every row is serialised to Python and back.

2.0 The data — with an explicit schema

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 2 · Class notes

2.0 The data — with an explicit schema (continued)

Explanation

A StructType is the schema written by hand: one StructField(name, type, nullable) per column. With an explicit schema Spark does not guess — marks is a 32-bit IntegerType instead of the inferred long.

In production, always give an explicit schema when you read files: inference costs an extra pass over the data and can guess wrong (a ZIP code read as a number loses its leading zero).

2Question

2.6 Combine conditions: &, | and ~ (continued)

4Explanation

Use & (and), | (or) and ~ (not) — not Python's and/or/not, which cannot combine Column objects.

Wrap every comparison in parentheses. In Python & binds tighter than ==, so F.col("branch") == "CSE" & F.col("city") == "Pune" is parsed wrongly and fails. Here & is evaluated before |, giving: (CSE and Pune) or marks > 90 — Amit, plus Arjun and Vikram. The second query counts the 11 students who are not from Delhi.

2.9 Sort: orderBy, asc and desc (continued)

4Explanation

orderBy (alias sort) takes columns with .asc() / .desc(). Here branches go A→Z and, inside each branch, marks go high→low.

Sorting the whole DataFrame is a wide operation: Spark samples the data, range-partitions it and sorts each partition. Sort only when you need ordered output.

NULLs come first in ascending order and last in descending order. Use asc_nulls_last() or desc_nulls_first() to choose.

4Explanation

2.13 Several columns at once: withColumns and lit (continued)

4Explanation

withColumns (Spark 3.3+) adds or replaces several columns from one dict — one plan step instead of a chain of withColumn calls.

F.lit(value) wraps a plain Python value as a Column. You need it whenever a constant has to be a column — a fixed label, a default, a flag.

Calling withColumn in a long Python loop (hundreds of times) builds a huge plan and slows planning. Build the expressions in a list and use one select or withColumns.

Chapter 2 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 2

  1. DataFrames are immutable: every transformation returns a new DataFrame; assign it to a variable or chain the calls.
  2. Name columns with a string, F.col("x") or df.x. Use df.x when two joined tables share a name.
  3. select picks and computes columns, withColumn / withColumns add or replace, withColumnRenamed renames, drop removes (silently ignores unknown names).

  4. filter = where. Combine with &, |, ~ and wrap each comparison in parentheses.

    SQL PySpark
    WHERE a = 1 AND b > 2 .filter((F.col("a") == 1) & (F.col("b") > 2))
    WHERE city IN ('Pune','Delhi') .filter(F.col("city").isin("Pune", "Delhi"))
    WHERE marks BETWEEN 80 AND 90 .filter(F.col("marks").between(80, 90))
    WHERE name LIKE 'A%' .filter(F.col("name").like("A%"))
    SELECT DISTINCT branch .select("branch").distinct()
    ORDER BY marks DESC .orderBy(F.col("marks").desc())

  5. F.lit() turns a Python constant into a column; F.expr() / selectExpr accept SQL text.

  6. distinct() compares whole rows; dropDuplicates([cols]) keeps an arbitrary row per key.
  7. Give an explicit schema (StructType or DDL string) for real data.
  8. df.createOrReplaceTempView("name") + spark.sql("SELECT …") gives the same result and the same plan as the DataFrame API.
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Deep dive: columns, types and ANSI mode

Small details that cause the most confusing bugs in week 2.

  • Spark 4 runs in ANSI mode: bad casts fail loudly
  • The same cast without try_ fails the whole job
  • Spark types you will meet

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 2 · Deep dive

Spark 4 runs in ANSI mode: bad casts fail loudly

Explanation

Since Spark 4.0, spark.sql.ansi.enabled is true: a cast that cannot succeed ("abc" → int), an integer overflow or a division by zero raises an error instead of quietly returning NULL.

When bad values are expected, use try_cast (or try_divide, try_add): they return NULL for the bad row and keep going.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 2 · Deep dive

The same cast without try_ fails the whole job

Explanation

One bad string anywhere in a billion rows stops the job. That is the point of ANSI mode: silent NULLs used to hide data-quality problems until a report was wrong.

Read the error class in brackets (CAST_INVALID_INPUT) — Spark 4 error messages name the exact cause and suggest the fix.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 2 · Deep dive

Spark types you will meet

Spark type Python value DDL name Note
IntegerType / LongType int INT / BIGINT Python ints are inferred as long
DoubleType float DOUBLE Use DecimalType for money
DecimalType(p, s) decimal.Decimal DECIMAL(10,2) Exact arithmetic
StringType str STRING
BooleanType bool BOOLEAN
DateType / TimestampType date / datetime DATE / TIMESTAMP Timestamps follow the session time zone
ArrayType, MapType, StructType list, dict, Row ARRAY<…>, MAP<…>, STRUCT<…> Chapter 8
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 2 · Deep dive

Why parentheses matter in filters

Explanation

Python evaluates "CSE" & F.col("marks") first, because & binds tighter than == and >. What is left, a == b > 80, is a Python chained comparison, which needs a True/False value from a Column — and PySpark refuses with CANNOT_CONVERT_COLUMN_INTO_BOOL.

The fix is always the same: (F.col("branch") == "CSE") & (F.col("marks") > 80).

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

3.0 The raw files on disk

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.0 The raw files on disk (continued)

Explanation

The CSV has a header, a quoted value with a space ("Navi Mumbai"), one malformed amount (abc) and one short row with a missing column — the problems every real file has.

ls() is a small helper used on later slides to show which files Spark writes. Spark's part-file names contain a long random ID, which the helper shortens to ….

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.1 Read a CSV with no options

Explanation

With no options Spark reads the header line as data, names the columns _c0, _c1, … and makes every column a string. CSV carries no types, so Spark does not guess unless asked.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.2 Use the header and let Spark infer types

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.2 Use the header and let Spark infer types (continued)

Explanation

header takes the column names from the first line. inferSchema scans the data to guess types: order_id became an integer and order_date a date — but amount stayed a string because of abc.

Inference also costs a full extra pass over the files. Fine for exploring; avoid it in pipelines.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.3 Give the schema yourself

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.3 Give the schema yourself (continued)

Explanation

With an explicit schema there is no inference pass and the types are what you decided. In the default PERMISSIVE mode the value Spark cannot parse becomes NULL (abc → NULL amount) and the missing field in row 7 becomes NULL too.

Silently NULL may be acceptable — or may hide a broken feed. The next slides catch the bad rows instead.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.4 Keep the broken lines for inspection (_corrupt_record)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.4 Keep the broken lines for inspection (_corrupt_record) (continued)

Explanation

Add a string column named _corrupt_record to the schema and Spark fills it with the raw text of every line it could not parse. Send those rows to a quarantine table and the clean rows onward.

The cache() is required: Spark refuses to query only the corrupt-record column straight from the file, because the result would depend on which columns are read.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.5 Skip bad lines, or fail on them: DROPMALFORMED and FAILFAST

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.5 Skip bad lines, or fail on them: DROPMALFORMED and FAILFAST (continued)

Explanation

DROPMALFORMED silently removes lines that do not fit the schema — rows 6 and 7 are gone. FAILFAST raises an error at the first bad line, which is what you want when a broken feed must stop the pipeline.

Note that count() alone may still report 7, because Spark can count lines without parsing them; collecting the rows forces the parse.

Pick the mode on purpose: PERMISSIVE + _corrupt_record for "keep going and quarantine", FAILFAST for "this file must be perfect".
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.6 Write Parquet and read it back

Explanation

A DataFrame is written as a folder, not a single file: one part-… file per partition plus an empty _SUCCESS marker that says the job finished.

Parquet stores the schema inside the files, so reading it back needs no options and the types are exact. It is columnar and compressed (snappy by default) — the standard format for analytics.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.7 Save modes: errorifexists, overwrite, append

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.7 Save modes: errorifexists, overwrite, append (continued)

Explanation

append adds new files next to the old ones (5 → 10 rows). overwrite replaces the whole folder (back to 5). The default mode errorifexists refuses to write into an existing path; ignore would silently skip the write.

Overwrite deletes the old data before the new data is safely written — if the job fails half-way, the old data is gone. Table formats such as Delta Lake make it atomic.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.8 Partition the output by a column (partitionBy)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.8 Partition the output by a column (partitionBy) (continued)

Explanation

partitionBy creates one sub-folder per value: month=2026-01/city=Pune/…. The partition columns are stored in the folder names, not inside the files.

Choose low-cardinality columns that queries filter on — date, month, country. Partitioning by a high-cardinality column (customer ID) creates millions of tiny folders.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.9 Read only the partitions you need (partition pruning)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.9 Read only the partitions you need (partition pruning) (continued)

Explanation

Spark rebuilds month and city from the folder names. The plan shows PartitionFilters: the filter is applied to folder names before any file is opened, so only month=2026-01/city=Pune is read — partition pruning.

On a table with 3 years of daily partitions, filtering one day reads about 0.1% of the data.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.10 Control the number of output files: coalesce and repartition

Explanation

The number of output files equals the number of partitions at write time. repartition(n) shuffles into exactly n partitions; coalesce(n) merges partitions without a shuffle (only to fewer partitions).

coalesce(1) gives one file but makes one task write everything — fine for a small export, a bottleneck for big data.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.11 JSON: one object per line, or a whole document

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.11 JSON: one object per line, or a whole document (continued)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.11 JSON: one object per line, or a whole document (continued)

Explanation

By default Spark expects JSON Lines: one complete object per line. It infers the schema from all fields seen, so amount exists with NULL for the click event, and the columns come out sorted by name.

A pretty-printed file or a top-level array spans many lines — read it with multiLine=True (one file is then parsed by one task).

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.12 Which file did each row come from? (_metadata)

Explanation

Every file-based DataFrame has a hidden _metadata struct (Spark 3.3+) with file_path, file_name, file_size and file_modification_time. Select it explicitly when you need lineage — which file a bad row came from.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.13 Write CSV for people (header, single file)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.13 Write CSV for people (header, single file) (continued)

Explanation

CSV is for handing data to people and other tools, not for storage: no types, no compression, no schema. Spark still writes a folder; coalesce(1) makes it a single part file you can rename.

Dates and doubles are written as text in Spark's default format.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Raw landing = the Bronze layer

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.14 Land the raw file as Bronze

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.14 Land the raw file as Bronze (continued)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Class notes

3.14 Land the raw file as Bronze (continued)

Explanation

Bronze rules: keep every row, keep every value as text (the bad abc and the short row 7 are still here — nothing is lost), add lineage columns (_source_file, _ingest_date), and only ever append, partitioned by load date.

Parsing, typing and cleaning happen in the next layer, Silver (Chapter 4). If a cleaning rule turns out to be wrong, Silver can always be rebuilt from Bronze. Chapter 12 makes these layers Delta tables.

The fixed _ingest_date keeps these notes reproducible. In a real job it is the run date passed by the scheduler, or F.current_timestamp() for a load timestamp.
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 3

  1. spark.read.format(...).option(...).schema(...).load(path) — or shortcuts .csv(), .json(), .parquet().
  2. CSV: set header, and give an explicit schema (DDL string) instead of inferSchema in pipelines.

  3. Bad records:

    mode Bad line becomes Use for
    PERMISSIVE (default) NULLs (+ raw text in _corrupt_record) keep going, quarantine bad rows
    DROPMALFORMED dropped silently rarely — data loss is invisible
    FAILFAST an error feeds that must be perfect

  4. Writes produce a folder of part- files + _SUCCESS. One file per partition.

  5. Save modes: errorifexists (default), overwrite, append, ignore.
  6. partitionBy(cols) → col=value/ folders; filters on those columns are pruned (PartitionFilters in the plan). Use low-cardinality columns.
  7. Parquet stores the schema, is columnar and compressed — use it (or Delta/Iceberg) for storage; CSV/JSON for exchange.
  8. coalesce(n) reduces files without a shuffle; repartition(n) shuffles to exactly n.
  9. _metadata.file_name tells you which file each row came from.
  10. Bronze = raw landing: all columns as received, lineage columns added, append-only, partitioned by load date.
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Deep dive: why Parquet is faster

Column pruning, predicate pushdown, file size — measured here, not claimed.

  • Same data: CSV vs Parquet on disk
  • Column pruning and predicate pushdown in the plan

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Deep dive

Same data: CSV vs Parquet on disk

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Deep dive

Same data: CSV vs Parquet on disk (continued)

Explanation

Parquet stores each column together, so repeated values (store, the constant day) compress extremely well with dictionary and run-length encoding. Typical real tables shrink 5–10× compared with CSV — less to read from disk and the network.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Deep dive

Column pruning and predicate pushdown in the plan

Explanation

ReadSchema: struct<id:bigint,amount:int> — only 2 of 4 columns are read from disk (column pruning). PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(amount), GreaterThan(amount,990)] — the filter is handed to the Parquet reader, which skips whole row groups whose min/max statistics cannot match (predicate pushdown).

CSV can do neither: every byte of every line must be read and parsed.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 3 · Deep dive

Reading from a database (JDBC)

Explanation

Not run in these notes (it needs a PostgreSQL server and its JDBC driver jar). Without partitionColumn / numPartitions Spark reads the whole table through one connection in one task; with them it opens 8 connections, each reading a range of order_id.

Filters and column selections are pushed down to the database as a WHERE clause and column list. Never hard-code passwords — read them from the environment or a secrets manager.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

4.6 Round the salaries: round, bround, floor, ceil (continued)

4Explanation

round(col, scale) rounds half up; a negative scale rounds to tens, hundreds, thousands. floor always goes down and ceil always up; both return integers (long).

bround rounds half to even (banker's rounding): bround(2.5) = 2, bround(3.5) = 4. It avoids an upward bias when you round millions of values.

4.10 Date arithmetic: datediff, months_between, add_months (continued)

4Explanation

datediff(end, start) counts days; months_between returns fractional months, so whole years = floor(months / 12). date_add adds days and add_months adds calendar months — adding 12 months to 2024-02-29 gives 2025-02-28 because the result is clamped to the last valid day.

A fixed reference date keeps the notes reproducible; in real code use F.current_date().

Without .otherwise, rows that match nothing get NULL. Here the NULL salary falls through to "Unknown".

4.17 Turn junk into NULL: nullif and NULL-safe equality (continued)

4Explanation

nullif(a, b) returns NULL when a = b, otherwise a — the standard way to turn a known junk value into NULL.

eqNullSafe is SQL's <=>: it treats two NULLs as equal and never returns NULL, so it gives true/false for every row.

4.18 One cleaning function, written as Silver (continued)

4Explanation

Silver is where raw data becomes trustworthy: names fixed, text standardised, real date and double types, invalid values (the 5-digit phone) turned into NULL, a default for missing departments, and one row per key.

All the rules live in one function, so they are easy to read, test (Chapter 14) and re-run on the Bronze data whenever a rule changes. Notice salary stays NULL for employee 104: Silver cleans data; it does not invent values that were never recorded.

Chapter 4 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 4

  1. All built-ins live in pyspark.sql.functions (F) and run in the JVM. Look there before writing a UDF.
  2. Strings: trim, lower, upper, initcap, length, concat_ws (skips NULLs), split(...).getItem(i), substring (1-based), lpad, regexp_replace, regexp_extract.
  3. Numbers: round (half up), bround (half even), floor, ceil; Spark 4 ANSI mode makes division by zero an error — use try_divide.

  4. Dates: parse with to_date(col, "yyyy-MM-dd") (MM = month, mm = minute).

    Need Function
    Part of a date year, month, dayofmonth, quarter, dayofweek
    Difference datediff(end, start), months_between
    Shift date_add, date_sub, add_months
    Bucket date_trunc("month", c) (timestamp), trunc(c, "month") (date)
    Format as text date_format(c, "dd MMM yyyy")

  5. F.when(...).when(...).otherwise(...) = CASE WHEN; first true branch wins; no otherwise → NULL.

  6. Test NULL with isNull() / isNotNull(), never == None.
  7. fillna / coalesce fill, dropna(subset=, thresh=) drops, nullif creates NULLs, eqNullSafe compares NULLs safely.
  8. Silver = Bronze after cleaning: one function of trim/case/regex/cast/NULL rules, typed columns, one row per key.
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 4 · Deep dive

Deep dive: functions that surprise people

Three behaviours that look like bugs until you know the rule.

  • Division by zero: error in ANSI mode, NULL with try_divide
  • Date patterns: MM is month, mm is minute
  • Why NULL > 0 is not false
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 4 · Deep dive

Division by zero: error in ANSI mode, NULL with try_divide

Explanation

try_divide returns NULL for the row with b = 0 and the query succeeds. Plain / raises DIVIDE_BY_ZERO because Spark 4 runs in ANSI mode.

Older tutorials say "division by zero returns NULL in Spark" — that was the pre-4.0 default.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 4 · Deep dive

Date patterns: MM is month, mm is minute

Explanation

With mm the formatter prints minutes — 00, because a date has no time part. Nothing fails; the report is silently wrong. Always use capital MM for months.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 4 · Deep dive

Why NULL > 0 is not false

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 4 · Deep dive

Why NULL > 0 is not false (continued)

Explanation

For the NULL row x > 0 is NULL, so it lands in neither the filter nor its negation: 1 + 1 rows out of 3. In when, NULL is treated like false and falls to otherwise.

When a filter and its opposite do not add up to the total row count, a NULL is hiding in the condition.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

5.4 Only the regions above ₹20,000 (HAVING) (continued)

4Explanation

There is no having method: a filter after agg is HAVING, because it runs on the aggregated rows. A filter before groupBy is WHERE — it removes order lines before they are summed.

Spark's optimiser places each filter correctly in the plan; you only need the right position in your code.

2Question

5.5 Distinct counts: countDistinct vs approx_count_distinct (continued)

4Explanation

countDistinct is exact but expensive on big data: Spark must keep every distinct value. approx_count_distinct uses the HyperLogLog++ sketch — a small fixed amount of memory, about 5% error by default, and exact on small data like this.

On billions of rows (daily active users, unique visitors), the approximate version is often 10× faster.

2Question

5.6 Conditional aggregation: sum(when) and count_if (continued)

4Explanation

Putting when inside an aggregate filters per column instead of per query — several "filtered totals" in one pass. This is SQL's SUM(CASE WHEN …) / COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …).

In the avg there is no otherwise, so non-Fashion rows become NULL and avg ignores them — the average is over Fashion orders only. With otherwise(0) the zeros would drag it down.

5.7 Keep the values, not just the count: collect_list and collect_set (continued)

4Explanation

collect_list gathers every value into an array (duplicates kept, order not guaranteed); collect_set removes duplicates. Wrap with array_sort for a stable order.

Both build the whole array on one executor, so never collect_list a group with millions of values.

5.14 Build a Gold table: monthly revenue per region (continued)

4Explanation

Gold tables answer a business question directly — here "how much did each region sell each month?" — at the grain the consumer needs (one row per month × region), with clear names and rounded values.

A dashboard reads 10 rows instead of re-aggregating millions of order lines on every refresh. Partitioning by month lets it read only the months it shows — and, as in Chapter 3, the partition column comes back as the last column when the table is read.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 5 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 5

  1. df.agg(...) aggregates the whole table into one row; df.groupBy(keys).agg(...) returns one row per group.
  2. Always alias aggregates. count("*") counts rows; count(col), sum, avg, min, max ignore NULLs.
  3. WHERE = filter before groupBy; HAVING = filter after agg.

  4. sum(when(cond, x)) / count_if(cond) give several filtered totals in one pass.

    SQL PySpark
    GROUP BY a HAVING SUM(x) > 10 .groupBy("a").agg(F.sum("x").alias("s")).filter("s > 10")
    COUNT(DISTINCT x) F.countDistinct("x") (exact) / F.approx_count_distinct("x")
    SUM(CASE WHEN c THEN x ELSE 0 END) F.sum(F.when(c, F.col("x")).otherwise(0))
    STRING_AGG / ARRAY_AGG F.collect_list, F.collect_set
    GROUP BY ROLLUP(a, b) .rollup("a", "b")
    GROUP BY CUBE(a, b) .cube("a", "b")
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 5 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 5 (continued)

  1. pivot(col, [values]) — list the values to save a job; unpivot reverses it.
  2. Every groupBy is a shuffle; partial aggregation before the shuffle keeps it cheap for sum/count, but not for collect_list or exact distinct counts.
  3. Gold = business-ready aggregates at the grain a report needs, written once and read many times.
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

2Question

Two-phase aggregation in the plan (continued)

4Explanation

Read it bottom-up: HashAggregate(partial_sum) sums inside each partition first, the Exchange shuffles only one row per region per partition, and the top HashAggregate adds the partial sums.

That is why sum, count, min, max and avg scale well — the shuffle carries partial results, not raw rows (the same idea as a combiner in MapReduce).

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

2Question

countDistinct needs an extra aggregation (continued)

4Explanation

An exact distinct count cannot be pre-summed: Spark first groups by (region, product) to remove duplicates, then counts per region — more HashAggregate steps and a second shuffle.

With high-cardinality columns this is where jobs slow down. Use approx_count_distinct when a small error is acceptable.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 5 · Deep dive

NULL keys form their own group

Explanation

All NULL keys are grouped together (as in SQL). But count("k") is 0 for that group, because count(col) skips NULLs — use count("*") to count the rows.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Concept

Why can countDistinct be much slower than sum on big data?

B. Sums can be pre-aggregated per partition; distinct values must be deduplicated across all partitions, which needs extra aggregation and shuffling.

df.rollup("region", "category") — what does a row with region = NULL and category = NULL hold?

6.4 Customers who never ordered (left_anti)

3Code

4Explanation

A left anti join returns left rows that have no match — SQL NOT EXISTS. Only the left table's columns come back.

It is cleaner and faster than "left join, then filter order_id IS NULL", and unlike NOT IN it is not broken by the NULL cust_id in orders.

Chapter 6 · Class notes

6.11 NULL keys never match — unless you ask (eqNullSafe)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 6 · Class notes

6.11 NULL keys never match — unless you ask (eqNullSafe) (continued)

Explanation

With ==, a NULL key never equals anything, not even another NULL, so only k = 1 matches. eqNullSafe (SQL <=>) treats NULL as equal to NULL.

Here the condition uses a.k and b.k: the df.col style is how you tell two same-named columns apart without aliases.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 6 · Class notes

6.12 Stack rows from two tables: union and unionByName

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 6 · Class notes

6.12 Stack rows from two tables: union and unionByName (continued)

Explanation

union matches columns by position, like SQL UNION ALL. The store table lists channel before city, so its row lands with city = store and channel = Delhi. Both columns are strings, so nothing fails — the data is just wrong.

Use unionByName. With allowMissingColumns=True it also fills columns missing on one side with NULL. Neither removes duplicates; add distinct() for SQL UNION.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 6 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 6

  1. left.join(right, on, how) — on as a name or list of names keeps one key column; an expression keeps both, so alias the DataFrames.

  2. Join types:

    how Keeps SQL
    inner matching pairs only INNER JOIN
    left / right all of one side + matches LEFT / RIGHT JOIN
    full everything from both sides FULL OUTER JOIN
    left_semi left rows with a match (no duplicates, left columns only) EXISTS / IN
    left_anti left rows without a match NOT EXISTS
    crossJoin every pairing CROSS JOIN

  3. One-to-many joins repeat the "one" side; check row counts before and after a join.

  4. NULL keys never match with ==; use eqNullSafe if NULL should equal NULL.
  5. Self joins need alias on both copies.
  6. union is by position, unionByName by name — prefer unionByName.
  7. Joins are wide transformations: both sides shuffle on the key unless one side is small enough to broadcast.
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

2Question

In-memory tables: Spark cannot measure them, so it sort-merges (continued)

4Explanation

Read bottom-up: both sides are shuffled on cust_id (two Exchange hashpartitioning lines), each partition is sorted, and the sorted streams are merged — a SortMergeJoin. It works at any size but costs two shuffles and two sorts.

These DataFrames were built with createDataFrame, so Spark has no size statistics for them and assumes they are large. Tiny as they are, it does not dare to broadcast.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 6 · Deep dive

Tables read from files: Spark knows the size and broadcasts

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 6 · Deep dive

Tables read from files: Spark knows the size and broadcasts (continued)

Explanation

Read from Parquet, Spark knows each table's size on disk. customers is far below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (10 MB by default), so the plan becomes a BroadcastHashJoin: the small side is sent whole to every executor (BroadcastExchange) and orders is not shuffled at all.

That is the fastest join Spark has. Note also PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(cust_id)] — the NULL-key filter is pushed into the Parquet reader.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Force it with a broadcast hint (continued)

4Explanation

F.broadcast(df) tells Spark to broadcast that side whatever its estimated size — exactly the fix for the in-memory case two slides back, or for any table whose size Spark cannot estimate after complex transformations.

Never broadcast a table that does not fit comfortably in executor memory: every executor gets a full copy.

Chapter 6 · Deep dive

The ambiguous column error

Explanation

With an expression condition both cust_id columns survive, and a bare "cust_id" cannot pick one: AMBIGUOUS_REFERENCE. Fix it by joining on the name (on="cust_id"), by selecting orders.cust_id, or by aliasing the DataFrames.

7.0 The data — purchases per customer

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 7 · Class notes

7.0 The data — purchases per customer (continued)

Explanation

Ten purchases by four customers. A window function computes a value for each row from a group of related rows (its window) without collapsing them — unlike groupBy, which returns one row per group.

A window is described with Window.partitionBy(...) (which rows belong together), .orderBy(...) (their order) and optionally a frame (rowsBetween / rangeBetween). Then F.some_function().over(window) uses it.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

4Explanation

The same pattern deduplicates data: order by "latest first" and keep rn == 1 to keep the newest record per key.

4Explanation

Chapter 7 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 7

  1. Window.partitionBy(...).orderBy(...) defines the window; F.fn().over(window) applies it. Rows are not collapsed.

  2. Ranking (row_number, rank, dense_rank, percent_rank, ntile) needs an orderBy.

    Values 300, 200, 200, 100 row_number rank dense_rank
    300 1 1 1
    200 2 2 2
    200 3 2 2
    100 4 4 3

  3. Top-N per group / dedup: add row_number() then filter(rn <= N) — you cannot filter a window function in the same select.

  4. lag looks back, lead looks forward; edges get NULL unless you give a default.
  5. Frames: rowsBetween(start, end) counts rows, rangeBetween uses values (e.g. seconds for "last 30 days").
  6. With orderBy the default frame ends at the current row → last() returns the current row. Use unboundedFollowing for the partition's real last value.
  7. A window without partitionBy puts all data in one partition — aggregate first or add a partition key.
  8. Every window with partitionBy costs a shuffle + sort by (partition keys, order keys).
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 7 · Deep dive

Gaps and islands: streaks of consecutive days (continued)

Explanation

Subtract the row number from the date: for consecutive days both go up by 1, so the difference (grp) stays constant inside a streak and jumps when there is a gap. Group by it to get each streak's start, end and length.

u1 has a 3-day streak and a 2-day streak; u2 never logged in two days in a row.

Chapter 7 · Deep dive

Sessionization: a new session after 30 minutes of silence (continued)

Explanation

Two windows: lag measures the gap to the previous click, and a running sum of the "new session" flags numbers the sessions. Every gap over 30 minutes starts session 2, 3, …

This is how web analytics builds sessions from raw click logs.

Chapter 8 · Class notes

8.0 The data — nested, like real JSON (continued)

Explanation

Spark columns can hold more than single values:

  • STRUCT — a fixed set of named fields (customer.name), like a nested JSON object.
  • ARRAY — a list of values of one type (items).
  • MAP — key → value pairs whose keys vary per row (meta).

events.payload holds raw JSON text, as it arrives from Kafka or an API log; this chapter parses it.

8.3 Inspect arrays: size, array_contains, element_at (continued)

4Explanation

size counts elements (0 for an empty array). array_contains tests membership. element_at(col, 1) takes the first element — 1-based, negative positions count from the end — while col[0] / getItem(0) is 0-based.

Order 3 has no items. In Spark 4 (ANSI mode) element_at past the end raises an error, so this uses try_element_at, which returns NULL. For 0-based access, items[0] also fails on an empty array; F.get(col, 0) returns NULL instead.

Chapter 8 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 8

  1. Three complex types: STRUCT (fixed named fields), ARRAY (list of one type), MAP (varying keys).
  2. Struct fields: "s.field", F.col("s.field"), or select("s.*") to flatten one level.
  3. Arrays: size, array_contains, element_at (1-based) vs getItem (0-based), array_distinct, sort_array, array_join.
  4. explode drops rows with empty/NULL arrays; explode_outer keeps them; posexplode adds the position.
  5. Higher-order functions transform, filter, aggregate, exists run in the JVM — the lambda is not Python at run time.
  6. JSON: from_json(col, schema) for many fields, get_json_object(col, "$.path") for one, to_json to write JSON.

  7. Re-nest with F.struct + collect_list — the inverse of explode.

    Need Function
    Array → rows explode, explode_outer, posexplode
    Rows → array collect_list, collect_set
    Text → struct from_json
    Struct → text to_json
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Deep dive: nested data in practice

The traps that appear when you flatten real JSON.

  • Exploding two arrays multiplies the rows
  • Malformed JSON becomes NULL, not an error

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 8 · Deep dive

Exploding two arrays multiplies the rows

Explanation

Two explodes in a row build a cross product: 2 × 2 = 4 rows, pairing every x with every y. When the arrays are parallel (element i of one belongs with element i of the other), arrays_zip them first and explode once.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 8 · Deep dive

Malformed JSON becomes NULL, not an error

Explanation

With the default PERMISSIVE mode a document that cannot be parsed returns a struct of NULLs instead of failing the job. Count those rows after parsing; silent data loss is the usual result of a schema mismatch.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 8 · Deep dive

Flatten every struct automatically

Explanation

The schema is ordinary Python data (df.schema.fields), so you can write helpers that walk it. This one flattens one level of structs with prefixed names; call it again for deeper nesting.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 9 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 9

  1. df.createOrReplaceTempView("name") → query it with spark.sql("…"). Views store no data.
  2. spark.sql returns a DataFrame — chain Python methods on it, or register results as new views.
  3. SQL and the DataFrame API produce the same plan: choose by readability, not speed.
  4. Use parameters: spark.sql("… WHERE x = :v", args={"v": 5}). Never f-string user input into SQL.

  5. spark.sql("SELECT … FROM {df}", df=my_df) uses a DataFrame without creating a view.

    Object Lives Visible to Stores data?
    Temp view Session That session No
    Global temp view (global_temp.x) Application All sessions No
    Table (saveAsTable) Until dropped Everyone using the catalog Yes (files)

  6. spark.catalog / SHOW TABLES / DESCRIBE TABLE inspect the metastore.

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.1 Read a real plan: explain(mode="formatted") (continued)

Explanation

formatted prints a short operator tree first, then the details of each numbered node underneath — far easier to read than the default one-line form.

Find, from the bottom: two Scan parquet nodes with pushed filters, the BroadcastHashJoin (stores is small), partial and final HashAggregate around one Exchange — exactly one shuffle for the whole report.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.2 How many partitions after a shuffle? (spark.sql.shuffle.partitions)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.2 How many partitions after a shuffle? (spark.sql.shuffle.partitions) (continued)

Explanation

After every shuffle Spark uses spark.sql.shuffle.partitions partitions — 200 by default, whatever the data size. Without AQE, 500 small groups are spread over 200 tiny partitions = 200 tasks.

With Adaptive Query Execution (on by default since Spark 3.2) Spark measures the shuffle output at run time and coalesces small partitions — here into a single one, because the whole result is tiny.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.3 AQE rewrites the plan while the query runs

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.3 AQE rewrites the plan while the query runs (continued)

Explanation

Before running, the plan says isFinalPlan=false. After an action, explain shows the Final Plan next to the Initial Plan. The AQEShuffleRead coalesced node is where AQE merged the 200 shuffle partitions.

AQE does three things at run time: coalesces small shuffle partitions, switches join strategy (sort-merge → broadcast) when one side turns out small, and splits skewed partitions in joins.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.4 repartition vs coalesce in the plan

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.4 repartition vs coalesce in the plan (continued)

Explanation

repartition(8) adds an Exchange RoundRobinPartitioning(8) — a full shuffle that produces evenly sized partitions. coalesce(2) shows a Coalesce 2 node and no Exchange: it glues existing partitions together on the same executors.

Use coalesce only to reduce partitions cheaply (before writing); use repartition to increase them or to fix uneven ones.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.5 Repartition by a column before a heavy operation

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.5 Repartition by a column before a heavy operation (continued)

Explanation

repartition(n, col) hash-partitions: all rows of one day land in the same partition (Exchange hashpartitioning(day, 4)). A later groupBy("day") or a write with partitionBy("day") then needs no further shuffle.

The row counts per partition are uneven — hashing 90 days into 4 buckets is not perfectly balanced.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.6 Reuse a result: cache() and the InMemoryRelation

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.6 Reuse a result: cache() and the InMemoryRelation (continued)

Explanation

cache() marks the DataFrame to be kept in executor memory (spilling to disk if needed: MEMORY_AND_DISK). It is lazy — the first action fills it. After that the plan reads from InMemoryTableScan instead of the Parquet files.

Cache only what you reuse several times in the same job (an iterative loop, several reports from one cleaned table). Caching something used once only adds work.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.7 Choose where to keep it: persist(StorageLevel) and unpersist

Explanation

persist(level) chooses the storage: MEMORY_ONLY, MEMORY_AND_DISK (what cache() uses for DataFrames), DISK_ONLY, or _2 variants that keep two copies.

Always unpersist() when done — cached blocks occupy executor memory that joins and aggregations need.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.8 Spot data skew: one key owns most of the rows

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.8 Spot data skew: one key owns most of the rows (continued)

Explanation

90% of the rows belong to store 7. Hash-partitioning by store_id sends all of them to one partition: one task processes 180,000+ rows while the others handle a few thousand.

In the Spark UI this shows up as one task running far longer than the median in a stage — the classic "99% done, waiting for the last task" job.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.9 Fix skew in an aggregation: salting

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.9 Fix skew in an aggregation: salting (continued)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.9 Fix skew in an aggregation: salting (continued)

Explanation

Add a random salt (0–7) and group by (store_id, salt) first: the hot key is split across 8 groups and 8 tasks. A second, tiny aggregation adds the 8 partial counts back together. The result is identical; the work is spread out.

The last table shows the partitions after salting: the hot key is spread over all 8 — the largest now holds about 49,000 rows instead of 180,000. Hash collisions keep it from being perfectly even. For joins, AQE's skew-join handling (spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled, on by default) splits oversized partitions automatically.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.10 Join strategy hints

Explanation

Hints override Spark's choice of join: broadcast, merge (sort-merge), shuffle_hash, shuffle_replicate_nl. Here shuffle_hash builds a hash table from the shuffled stores side instead of sorting both sides.

Use hints when you know something the optimiser cannot: missing statistics, or a side that is small after filtering.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.11 Built-in filters are pushed down; Python filters are not

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.11 Built-in filters are pushed down; Python filters are not (continued)

Explanation

With a built-in comparison, PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(amount), GreaterThan(amount,990)] — Parquet skips row groups that cannot match. With a Python UDF, PushedFilters: []: every row is read, sent to a Python worker (ArrowEvalPython — Spark 4.2 batches regular UDFs through Arrow) and back.

The same logic, written two ways, can differ by an order of magnitude. Chapter 11 covers UDFs properly.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Class notes

10.12 Check what the session is using

Explanation

These six settings explain most tuning conversations. maxPartitionBytes (128 MB) decides how many partitions a file read produces; autoBroadcastJoinThreshold is in bytes (10 MB).

Set them per job with spark.conf.set(...) or at submit time with --conf key=value.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 10

  1. Read plans bottom-up; count Exchange nodes (shuffles) first — they dominate cost.
  2. spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 200 by default; AQE coalesces small shuffle partitions, switches to broadcast joins and splits skewed partitions at run time.
  3. repartition(n[, col]) = full shuffle (balance, or co-locate a key); coalesce(n) = merge without shuffle (only to fewer).
  4. Join strategies: BroadcastHashJoin (small side ≤ 10 MB, no shuffle of the big side) → SortMergeJoin (two shuffles + sorts, any size). Hint with F.broadcast(df) or df.hint("…").
  5. cache() / persist(level) are lazy; cache only reused results and unpersist() afterwards.
  6. Skew = one partition much bigger than the rest. Fix with salting (aggregations) or AQE skew join (joins); isolate hot keys.
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 10 (continued)

  1. Keep work in the JVM: built-in functions get pushdown and code generation; Python UDFs get neither.

    Symptom in the Spark UI Likely cause First fix
    One task much slower than the rest Skew Salt the key / AQE skew join
    Thousands of tiny tasks Too many partitions / small files AQE coalescing, coalesce before write
    Spill to disk, OOM in a stage Partitions too large More shuffle partitions, repartition
    Big shuffle on a join with a small table No broadcast F.broadcast(small)
    Same stages computed twice Reused result not cached cache() then unpersist()

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Deep dive

Inside an executor's memory

Region Default share Holds
Reserved 300 MB Spark internals
Unified memory (spark.memory.fraction = 0.6 of the rest) 60% Execution (shuffles, joins, sorts, aggregations) and storage (cached data) — they borrow from each other
User memory 40% Your objects, UDF data structures
Overhead (spark.executor.memoryOverhead) max(384 MB, 10%) Off-heap, Python workers, native buffers

When execution needs more memory it can evict cached blocks; when neither fits, Spark spills to disk (slow but safe). "Container killed for exceeding memory limits" usually means the overhead was too small — common with Python UDFs and pandas, which live outside the JVM heap.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Deep dive

Sizing executors: a worked example

Step Rule of thumb 10 nodes × 16 cores × 64 GB
Cores per executor 4–5 (HDFS/S3 throughput, GC) 5
Executors per node (cores − 1 for OS) / 5 3
Total executors nodes × per node − 1 for the driver 29
Memory per executor (RAM − 1 GB) / executors per node, minus ~10% overhead ~19 GB heap
Parallelism total cores × 2–3 ~300–450 shuffle partitions

These are starting points, not laws. Target shuffle partitions of roughly 100–200 MB each, then let AQE coalesce. On Databricks or EMR Serverless much of this is managed for you, but the vocabulary is the same in every interview.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 10 · Deep dive

A tuning checklist, in order

  1. Read less: Parquet/Delta, select only needed columns, filter early on partition columns.
  2. Shuffle less: broadcast small tables, avoid unnecessary distinct / orderBy, aggregate before joining.
  3. Balance the work: check task-time spread in the Spark UI; salt or let AQE split skew.
  4. Right-size partitions: ~128–200 MB; AQE coalescing on; coalesce before writing small outputs.
  5. Stay in the JVM: built-ins and higher-order functions over UDFs; pandas UDFs when Python is unavoidable.
  6. Cache deliberately and unpersist.
  7. Only then: executor memory, cores and cluster size.
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

11.6 Vectorised: a pandas UDF (Series → Series) (continued)

4Explanation

A pandas UDF receives a whole batch of rows as a pandas.Series (thousands at a time, transferred with Apache Arrow) and returns a Series of the same length. The Python function runs once per batch, not once per row, so it is typically 10–100× faster than a row-at-a-time UDF.

The type hints pd.Series -> pd.Series tell Spark which kind of pandas UDF this is.

4Explanation

With a Series -> scalar signature the pandas UDF becomes an aggregate function usable in groupBy().agg(). Each group's values arrive as one Series.

Here: the rating weighted by price, which takes two columns — each arrives as its own Series. Use this for statistics Spark does not have built in. Two limits: all values of a group must fit in one Python worker's memory, and a pandas aggregate cannot be mixed with built-in aggregates such as F.avg in the same agg (INVALID_PANDAS_UDF_PLACEMENT) — which is why the mean here is a pandas UDF too.

Points to be Noted — Chapter 11 (continued)

  1. pandas UDFs move batches with Arrow and run once per batch:

    Tool Input → output Use for
    @udf value → value Small custom logic, no alternative
    @pandas_udf Series → Series column batch → column batch Vectorised maths, string work
    @pandas_udf Series → scalar group → one value Custom aggregates
    groupBy().applyInPandas group DataFrame → DataFrame Per-group models, complex pandas code
    mapInPandas batches → batches Load a model once per partition, score
    @udtf row → many rows Python table functions in SQL

  2. spark.udf.register / spark.udtf.register make them callable from SQL.

  3. toPandas() collects to the driver — only for small, aggregated results. Arrow makes it fast.
  4. df.pandas_api() / pyspark.pandas = pandas syntax executed by Spark.

Chapter 11 · Deep dive

Deep dive: what a UDF really costs

Where the time goes, and the two settings that matter.

  • The round trip of every Python UDF row
  • Arrow settings in this session
  • A wrong return type: a silent cast or a silent NULL
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 11 · Deep dive

The round trip of every Python UDF row

Step Where Cost
1. Serialise rows from Spark's internal format JVM executor CPU
2. Send them over a socket to a Python worker Executor → Python process I/O
3. Deserialise into Python objects, call your function Python worker Interpreter speed
4. Serialise the results and send them back Python → JVM I/O + CPU
5. Optimiser cannot see inside the function Catalyst No pushdown, no reordering

Arrow batching (pandas UDFs, and Arrow-optimised regular UDFs in recent Spark versions) shrinks steps 1–4 dramatically. Step 5 never goes away — that is why a built-in filter can skip whole files and a UDF filter cannot.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 11 · Deep dive

Arrow settings in this session

Explanation

maxRecordsPerBatch (10,000) is how many rows a pandas UDF receives per call. Lower it if each batch uses too much memory in Python; raise it for cheap per-row work.
