Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.0 A Spark session with Delta Lake

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.0 A Spark session with Delta Lake (continued)

Explanation

Delta Lake is an open table format: ordinary Parquet files plus a transaction log (_delta_log/) that records every change. The two config lines register Delta's SQL commands and catalog; configure_spark_with_delta_pip adds the matching Delta JARs to the session.

Databricks has Delta built in; on plain Spark you add the delta-spark package whose version matches your Spark version.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12

The medallion architecture in full

Chapters 3, 4 and 5 each built one layer with plain Parquet. Here are the rules for all three, and why Delta is the format teams use for them.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.1 Bronze, Silver, Gold — the rules of each layer

Bronze Silver Gold
Purpose Keep the data exactly as it arrived Clean, conformed, trustworthy records Answers to business questions
Typical content Raw rows as strings + _source_file, _ingest_date Typed columns, deduplicated, validated, one row per key Aggregates, KPIs, wide tables for BI and ML features
Write pattern Append only MERGE (upsert) by key, SCD2 for history Overwrite or MERGE per period
Data quality None — never reject Rules enforced, bad rows quarantined Business rules, reconciled totals
Who reads it Data engineers (replay, debugging) Engineers, analysts, data scientists Dashboards, reports, models, APIs
Built in Chapter 3 Chapter 4 Chapter 5

Data flows one way: Bronze → Silver → Gold. Because Bronze keeps everything, a bug in a Silver rule is fixed by changing the rule and re-running from Bronze — no source system has to re-send anything.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.2 Why plain Parquet folders are not enough

Problem with a Parquet folder What Delta's transaction log adds
A job dies half-way through an overwrite: the old data is gone, the new data is incomplete ACID transactions: a write commits fully or not at all
Correcting one customer means rewriting files by hand MERGE, UPDATE, DELETE
A bad load cannot be undone Time travel and RESTORE to an earlier version
Readers see files appear one by one during a write Readers always see the last committed version
A new column or wrong type silently enters the table Schema enforcement, and evolution only when you ask
Small files pile up after many appends OPTIMIZE compaction, VACUUM of old files

Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi solve the same problems with a similar design; the ideas in this chapter carry over. These notes use Delta because it ships with Databricks and has a pip package for local Spark.

4Explanation

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.5 Schema enforcement: unexpected columns are refused

Explanation

Plain Parquet would happily write files with an extra column and leave the folder inconsistent. Delta checks the incoming schema against the table's and refuses the write: DELTA_METADATA_MISMATCH.

That protects every Silver and Gold table from an upstream change nobody announced.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.6 Schema evolution, when you decide to allow it

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.6 Schema evolution, when you decide to allow it (continued)

Explanation

mergeSchema=true adds the new column to the table schema in the same commit. Existing rows read it as NULL. Evolution is a deliberate, recorded decision — visible in the history — not an accident.

12.7 UPDATE and DELETE on a lake table

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

12.7 UPDATE and DELETE on a lake table (continued)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.7 UPDATE and DELETE on a lake table (continued)

Explanation

update(condition, set) and delete(condition) change individual rows. Behind the scenes Delta rewrites only the data files that contain matching rows and commits "remove old file, add new file" to the log. The values in set are SQL expressions, so a string needs inner quotes: "'Pune'".

Chapter 12

MERGE: the upsert behind every Silver table

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.8 Upsert a batch of changes (MERGE)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.8 Upsert a batch of changes (MERGE) (continued)

Explanation

MERGE compares source rows with target rows on a key: matched rows are updated, not matched rows are inserted — one atomic commit. Amit moved to Bengaluru; Meera is new.

whenMatchedUpdateAll() / whenNotMatchedInsertAll() copy every column when the names match; whenNotMatchedBySourceDelete() also removes target rows missing from the source.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.9 The same MERGE in SQL

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.9 The same MERGE in SQL (continued)

Explanation

CREATE TABLE … USING DELTA LOCATION registers the existing folder under a name in the catalog — no data is copied — so SQL can say MERGE INTO customers. The extra condition s.updated_at > t.updated_at makes the merge ignore stale updates that arrive late — a common guard in real pipelines.

The columns are listed explicitly: UPDATE SET * / INSERT * would require the source to have every target column, including the email added on slide 12.6. The statement returns the merge metrics: rows affected, updated, deleted and inserted.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.10 SCD Type 1 vs Type 2

SCD Type 1 SCD Type 2
On change Overwrite the old value Close the old row, add a new row
History Lost Kept, with validity dates
Columns added None start_date, end_date, is_current
Question it can answer "Where does Amit live now?" "Where did Amit live when he placed the January order?"
Implemented by The MERGE on slide 12.8 The MERGE on the next slide

SCD = slowly changing dimension: attributes such as a customer's city that change rarely, but whose history matters for correct reporting. Revenue by city for January must use the city the customer had in January.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.11 SCD Type 2 with one MERGE

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.11 SCD Type 2 with one MERGE (continued)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.11 SCD Type 2 with one MERGE (continued)

Explanation

The trick is the staged source. Every update appears once with merge_key = customer_id: it matches the customer's current row, and if the city changed, that row is closed (is_current = false, end_date set). Changed customers appear a second time with merge_key = NULL, which never matches, so they are inserted as the new current version.

Result: Amit has a closed Bengaluru row (his city after slide 12.8) and a current Hyderabad row; Riya (already Pune) is untouched; Dev is new. Arjun was not in the batch and keeps his row.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12

Incremental loads

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.12 Load only what changed since last time (a high-water mark)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.12 Load only what changed since last time (a high-water mark) (continued)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.12 Load only what changed since last time (a high-water mark) (continued)

Explanation

A high-water mark is the largest updated_at already loaded. Each run reads only source rows newer than it and MERGEs them, so a changed order (102, corrected to 950) is updated in place and a new order (104) is inserted. Run 3 finds nothing new and changes nothing — the load is idempotent.

For files instead of a database, Structured Streaming with availableNow (Chapter 13) gives the same "only new data" behaviour through checkpoints.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.13 Pass changes downstream: the Change Data Feed

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.13 Pass changes downstream: the Change Data Feed (continued)

Explanation

With the Change Data Feed on, Delta records row-level changes. Reading with readChangeFeed returns each changed row with _change_type: insert, delete, or the update_preimage / update_postimage pair (before and after).

Gold jobs use it to update only the aggregates affected by changed Silver rows instead of recomputing everything.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12

Undo and maintenance

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.14 Undo a bad load: RESTORE

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.14 Undo a bad load: RESTORE (continued)

Explanation

restoreToVersion(n) (SQL: RESTORE TABLE … TO VERSION AS OF n) makes an old version current again. It is itself a new commit, so even the restore can be undone.

The old data files are still there because Delta only marks them as removed in the log; they are physically deleted later by VACUUM.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.15 Compact small files: OPTIMIZE, then VACUUM

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Class notes

12.15 Compact small files: OPTIMIZE, then VACUUM (continued)

Explanation

Frequent small appends (streaming, hourly loads) create many small files, and reading many small files is slow. OPTIMIZE rewrites them into fewer large ones in one commit; readers are not disturbed.

VACUUM then deletes data files no longer referenced by any version newer than the retention period (7 days by default). After vacuuming, time travel beyond that period is no longer possible — that is the trade-off.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 12

  1. Medallion: Bronze (raw, append-only, lineage) → Silver (clean, typed, MERGE by key) → Gold (business aggregates). Rebuild downstream from Bronze when rules change.
  2. Delta Lake = Parquet files + a _delta_log transaction log → ACID writes, time travel, MERGE/UPDATE/DELETE, schema enforcement.
  3. Write: df.write.format("delta").save(path); read: spark.read.format("delta").load(path); old versions: option("versionAsOf", n).
  4. Schema changes are refused unless you pass mergeSchema=true.
  5. MERGE = upsert: whenMatchedUpdate…, whenNotMatchedInsert…, whenNotMatchedBySourceDelete.
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 12 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 12 (continued)

  1. SCD1 overwrites; SCD2 closes the old row (end_date, is_current=false) and inserts a new one — one MERGE with a staged source (merge_key NULL for the new versions).
  2. Incremental loads: high-water mark on updated_at + MERGE → idempotent re-runs. The Change Data Feed passes row-level changes downstream.

  3. RESTORE undoes a bad load; OPTIMIZE compacts small files; VACUUM deletes unreferenced files (and limits time travel).

    Operation Python SQL
    History DeltaTable.forPath(spark, p).history() DESCRIBE HISTORY t
    Read old version .option("versionAsOf", 3) SELECT * FROM t VERSION AS OF 3
    Upsert dt.alias("t").merge(src.alias("s"), cond)…execute() MERGE INTO t USING s ON …
    Undo dt.restoreToVersion(3) RESTORE TABLE t TO VERSION AS OF 3
    Compact dt.optimize().executeCompaction() OPTIMIZE t

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.0 A folder that receives new files

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.0 A folder that receives new files (continued)

Explanation

Structured Streaming treats a stream as a table that keeps growing: every new record is a new row, and your query is re-run incrementally on the new rows only.

Here the stream source is a folder: each new JSON file is a new batch of orders. drop_file writes to a temporary name and renames it, because a file source must never see half-written files. The same code works with Kafka by changing only the readStream source.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.1 Read a stream: readStream with a schema

Explanation

spark.readStream returns a streaming DataFrame. Most of the DataFrame API — select, filter, withColumn, groupBy, joins — works on it unchanged.

A file stream requires a schema: Spark cannot infer one from data that has not arrived yet. Calling show() or count() directly on a streaming DataFrame is an error — results are produced by starting a query with writeStream.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.2 Start a query: writeStream, a sink, a trigger

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.2 Start a query: writeStream, a sink, a trigger (continued)

Explanation

writeStream needs a sink (memory here — for testing only; real sinks are files, Delta tables and Kafka), an output mode and a trigger.

availableNow=True processes all data available now and stops — perfect for scheduled "incremental batch" jobs and for reproducible notes. Without a trigger the query runs forever, starting a micro-batch as soon as the previous one finishes.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.3 Process only the new files: checkpoints

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.3 Process only the new files: checkpoints (continued)

Explanation

The checkpoint folder records which files were already processed (and, for stateful queries, the running state). Run 1 reads the 4 orders of batch1. Run 2 reads only the new file. Run 3 finds nothing new.

That is how a scheduled streaming job gets exactly-once results: restart it as often as you like, and each input file is processed once. Never share a checkpoint between two queries.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.4 A running aggregate: outputMode("complete")

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.4 A running aggregate: outputMode("complete") (continued)

Explanation

An aggregation keeps state — the running count and sum per city — between micro-batches. complete mode rewrites the whole result table after each batch.

append is not allowed for an aggregation without a watermark, because a city's total can still change when new orders arrive; Spark would refuse to start the query.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.5 Count per 10-minute window (event time)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.5 Count per 10-minute window (event time) (continued)

Explanation

F.window(timeColumn, "10 minutes") assigns each order to a 10-minute bucket by its event time — the ts inside the record — not by when Spark happened to read it. That keeps results correct when data arrives late or out of order.

window("ts", "10 minutes", "5 minutes") would make sliding windows that overlap.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.6 Late data and watermarks

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.6 Late data and watermarks (continued)

Explanation

A watermark of 10 minutes says: "events more than 10 minutes older than the latest event seen can be ignored". After batch2 the latest event is 10:31, so the watermark is 10:21 — windows ending before it are final, written once in append mode, and their state is dropped.

Order 6 (10:02) arrives after its window was finalised, so it is not counted: the 10:00–10:10 window still shows 3 orders. Without a watermark, Spark would have to keep every window's state forever.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.7 Write each micro-batch with batch code: foreachBatch

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.7 Write each micro-batch with batch code: foreachBatch (continued)

Explanation

foreachBatch(func) calls your function with each micro-batch as an ordinary batch DataFrame plus its batch ID. Inside, you can use any batch API: write to several sinks, MERGE into a Delta table, call an API, write to a JDBC database.

maxFilesPerTrigger=1 — an option of the source, set on readStream — makes each file its own micro-batch, so the three files produced three batches (4, 1 and 2 orders). availableNow respects such limits and simply runs as many batches as needed. Use batch_id to make writes idempotent if a batch is retried.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.8 Enrich a stream with a static table (stream–static join)

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.8 Enrich a stream with a static table (stream–static join) (continued)

Explanation

Joining a stream with a static DataFrame needs no state: each new order is looked up in the static table. The static side is re-read for every micro-batch, so updates to a dimension file are picked up.

Stream–stream joins are also supported but need watermarks on both sides to bound the state.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Class notes

13.9 Monitor a query: status and progress

Explanation

lastProgress (and recentProgress) report every micro-batch: rows read, input and processing rates, durations, watermark and state size. status says what the query is doing right now.

In production these numbers go to monitoring, and the Spark UI has a Structured Streaming tab with the same metrics as charts.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 13

  1. A stream is an unbounded table; Spark runs your query incrementally in micro-batches.
  2. spark.readStream… → transformations → writeStream.format(sink).outputMode(mode).trigger(…).start().
  3. File streams need an explicit schema. Upstream must write files atomically (write, then rename).

  4. Checkpoints store progress and state → exactly-once results across restarts. One checkpoint per query.

    Output mode Writes Allowed with
    append only new final rows no aggregation, or aggregation + watermark
    update rows that changed in this batch aggregations
    complete the whole result table aggregations only
    Trigger Behaviour
    default next micro-batch as soon as the last one ends
    processingTime="1 minute" one micro-batch per minute
    availableNow=True process everything available, then stop

  5. Group by event time with F.window(ts, "10 minutes"); bound state and late data with withWatermark(ts, "10 minutes").

  6. foreachBatch lets you use the full batch API (Delta MERGE, JDBC, several sinks) on each micro-batch.
  7. Monitor with lastProgress, status and the Structured Streaming tab of the Spark UI.

Reading from Kafka

Chapter 13 · Deep dive

Error: a streaming DataFrame cannot show()

Explanation

show, count and collect would need the whole, never-ending table. Start a query with writeStream instead — to the memory sink when you just want to look at results while developing.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 13 · Deep dive

Error: append mode on an aggregation without a watermark

Explanation

In append mode a row may be written only once, when it is final. A per-city count is never final in an endless stream, so Spark refuses at start-up. Use complete or update, or aggregate by event-time window with a watermark.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 14 · Class notes

14.7 Re-runs must be safe: dynamic partition overwrite

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 14 · Class notes

14.7 Re-runs must be safe: dynamic partition overwrite (continued)

Explanation

With the default (static) mode, overwrite deletes the whole folder — re-running one day would wipe every other day. With partitionOverwriteMode=dynamic, Spark replaces only the partitions present in the new data: 2026-03-02 was rewritten, 2026-03-01 kept.

That makes a daily job idempotent: running it twice for the same day gives the same result as running it once — the property every scheduler retry relies on.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 14 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 14

  1. Write transformations as pure functions DataFrame → DataFrame; chain them with df.transform(func). Keep I/O at the edges.
  2. Configuration (dates, paths, thresholds) comes from arguments or config files, not from the middle of the code.
  3. Test with pyspark.testing.assertDataFrameEqual / assertSchemaEqual and pytest; build tiny hand-made inputs with edge cases; share one SparkSession per test run.
  4. Run data-quality checks in one aggregation and fail the job before writing bad data.
  5. Make jobs idempotent: partitionOverwriteMode=dynamic + partitionBy(date), or MERGE into a table format.

  6. Log structured metrics (rows in/out/dropped) on the driver.

    Layer Typical content
    Bronze Raw data as received, append-only
    Silver Cleaned, typed, deduplicated
    Gold Business aggregates for reports and ML

Chapter 14 · Deep dive

A project layout that scales

Path Holds
src/orders_job/transforms.py Pure DataFrame → DataFrame functions
src/orders_job/io.py Readers and writers (paths, formats, schemas)
src/orders_job/main.py Parses arguments, builds the SparkSession, wires I/O and transforms
tests/conftest.py Session-scoped spark fixture for pytest
tests/test_transforms.py One test per transform, with edge cases
pyproject.toml Dependencies; build a wheel for the cluster

Only main.py knows about the outside world. Everything in transforms.py can be tested on a laptop in seconds.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 14 · Deep dive

Submitting the job to a cluster

Explanation

Not run in these notes (it needs a cluster). spark-submit starts the driver and executors, ships your code (--py-files takes a wheel or zip), and passes arguments to main.py. In cluster deploy mode the driver runs on the cluster, so the job survives your laptop disconnecting.

Schedulers (Airflow, Databricks Workflows, cron) call exactly this command once per day with a different --run-date.

Chapter 15 · Class notes

15.0 ShopKart's raw files for two days (continued)

Explanation

ShopKart is a small online shop. Every day its systems drop files into a landing folder: the day's orders (CSV) and new or changed customers (JSON), plus a one-off product catalogue. The generator has a fixed seed, so every run produces the same files.

The files contain the problems a real pipeline must handle: messy names and cities, inconsistent status text, a duplicated order, a non-numeric quantity, an order for a customer who does not exist, a customer who moves city on day 2, and a correction that cancels a day-1 order.

The goal: Bronze tables that keep everything, Silver tables you can trust, and Gold tables a dashboard can read — re-runnable day after day.

15.1 Bronze: land each file exactly as it arrived (continued)

Bronze keeps every line — 27 order lines, including both versions of order 1005, the two quantity and the unknown customer C99 — with every value as text, plus _source_file and _ingest_date. Orders and customers are appended day by day; the small product catalogue is simply overwritten.

Nothing is judged here. If tomorrow we discover a better way to parse a field, Bronze still has the original.

Chapter 15 · Class notes

15.4 Silver orders: validate, quarantine, deduplicate, MERGE (continued)

Explanation

Four rules, in order: cast with try_cast so a bad quantity becomes NULL instead of failing the job; validate — rows with no quantity or an unknown customer go to a quarantine table with a reason, not into the bin; deduplicate — one row per order_id, keeping the latest; MERGE by key, updating only when the incoming row is newer.

27 Bronze lines became 24 Silver orders: order 1005 arrived twice with different contents, so only the later line (18:00) was kept, and two rows were quarantined for someone to fix at the source.

15.7 The whole day as one function — then day 2 arrives (continued)

Explanation

The daily job is just the steps in order. A scheduler (Airflow, Databricks Workflows) calls run_day with the date; a failed day is re-run with the same date.

Day 2 added 15 Bronze order lines (14 new orders and one correction), 14 new Silver orders, and new Silver customer rows for the move and the new customer. The products step is not repeated: the catalogue did not change.

Chapter 15 · Class notes

15.10 Quality gates across the layers

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 15 · Class notes

15.10 Quality gates across the layers (continued)

Explanation

Every check should be zero: no duplicate keys, no invalid quantities, exactly one current version per customer, and Gold revenue that reconciles to Silver to the rupee. The job raises if any check fails, so a bad day never reaches the dashboard silently.

Add these checks to run_day and you have the capstone: a re-runnable, tested, history-keeping lakehouse pipeline.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 15 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 15

  1. Bronze: append raw files as text with _source_file and _ingest_date; never reject anything.
  2. Silver: cast with try_cast, validate, quarantine failures with a reason, deduplicate with row_number, MERGE by key (update only when newer).
  3. Customers are an SCD2 dimension: close the old version, insert the new — so facts can be joined to the version valid on their date.
  4. Gold: rebuild from Silver; join facts to SCD2 dimensions by key and date range; exclude cancelled orders.
  5. Wrap each layer in a function and the day in run_day(day) — schedulable, re-runnable, testable.
  6. Quality gates that must be zero (duplicates, invalid values, one current row, Gold reconciles to Silver) stop bad data before it reaches users.

  7. Delta time travel explains why a number changed between yesterday and today.

    Table Layer Write pattern
    bronze/orders, bronze/customers Bronze append per day
    silver/customers Silver SCD2 MERGE
    silver/orders Silver MERGE (upsert, newer wins)
    silver/orders_quarantine Silver append
    gold/daily_sales, gold/customer_360 Gold overwrite from Silver

Why does the Gold daily-sales join use the order date between start_date and end_date?

The day-2 file contains order 1003 again with status cancelled and a later timestamp. What does the Silver MERGE do?

B. whenMatchedUpdateAll(condition="s.order_ts > t.order_ts") applies newer versions of an existing order.

Chapter 15 · MCQ

Concept

run_day("2026-03-02") crashes after the Bronze step and is re-run. Which part could create duplicates?

C. Append-only Bronze would land the day twice. Real pipelines guard it: overwrite the day's partition (replaceWhere / dynamic overwrite) or record loaded files — Silver dedup then keeps results correct.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 15 · MCQ

Concept

Which check proves Gold is consistent with Silver?

B. Reconciling an aggregate back to its source is the standard Gold-layer test.

4Explanation

Two kinds of objects run all of MLlib. An Estimator learns from data with fit() and returns a model. A Transformer adds columns with transform().

StringIndexer is an estimator: fit counts the categories and orders them by frequency (most common → 0.0); the fitted model then maps text to numbers.

16.2 One-hot encode the category (continued)

4Explanation

An index such as 0, 1, 2 would wrongly tell a linear model that TwoYear is "twice" Yearly. One-hot encoding turns it into a vector with a single 1. Spark prints it as a sparse vector (size, [positions], [values]).

With 3 categories the vector has size 2: the last category is dropped (dropLast=True) because it is implied when the others are 0.

16.4 The whole recipe as a Pipeline (continued)

4Explanation

A Pipeline chains the stages; pipeline.fit(train) fits each estimator in order on the training data only and returns a PipelineModel that replays every step on new data.

That is what prevents data leakage: the scaler's mean and standard deviation, and the indexer's categories, are learned from the training set alone. randomSplit with a seed gives a reproducible 75/25 split.

16.6 How good is it? AUC and accuracy (continued)

4Explanation

AUC (area under the ROC curve) measures how well the predicted probabilities rank churners above non-churners: 0.5 is a coin toss, 1.0 is perfect. Accuracy is the share of correct 0/1 predictions.

The pivot is a confusion matrix: rows are the true label, columns the prediction. Off-diagonal cells are the mistakes — false alarms and missed churners.

16.9 Tune hyper-parameters: CrossValidator (continued)

4Explanation

ParamGridBuilder lists the combinations to try (3 × 2 = 6). CrossValidator fits every combination on 3 train/validation folds — 18 fits — and keeps the best by average AUC; cv_model.bestModel is refitted on all the training data.

Read the last line: strong L1 regularisation (regParam=1.0, elasticNetParam=1.0) pushed every coefficient to zero, so the model predicts the same probability for everyone — AUC 0.5, a coin toss. parallelism=2 trains two candidate models at the same time.

Chapter 16 · Summary

Points to be Noted — Chapter 16

  1. Estimator .fit(df) → Model (a Transformer) .transform(df) adds columns.
  2. Features must be one vector column: StringIndexer → OneHotEncoder → VectorAssembler (→ StandardScaler for linear models).
  3. Put every step in a Pipeline; fit it on the training data only to avoid leakage. Save/load the whole PipelineModel.
  4. randomSplit([0.75, 0.25], seed=…) for a reproducible split; seed tree models too.
  5. Evaluate with BinaryClassificationEvaluator (AUC), MulticlassClassificationEvaluator (accuracy, F1), RegressionEvaluator (RMSE); build a confusion matrix with a pivot.

  6. Tune with ParamGridBuilder + CrossValidator (or the cheaper TrainValidationSplit).

    Task Common MLlib classes
    Classification LogisticRegression, RandomForestClassifier, GBTClassifier
    Regression LinearRegression, RandomForestRegressor, GBTRegressor
    Clustering KMeans, BisectingKMeans

Chapter 16 · Deep dive

Deep dive: MLlib in a real project

When to use MLlib, and when to aggregate in Spark and train elsewhere.

  • MLlib, or Spark for features and scikit-learn for the model?
  • Data leakage: fit transformers on the training set only
Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 16 · Deep dive

MLlib, or Spark for features and scikit-learn for the model?

Situation Good choice
Training data does not fit on one machine MLlib (distributed training)
Training data fits in memory after aggregation Spark for features → toPandas() → scikit-learn / XGBoost
Many small models (one per store / product) groupBy().applyInPandas() with scikit-learn inside (Chapter 11)
Scoring a huge table with a model trained elsewhere mapInPandas / pandas UDF that loads the model once per partition
Deep learning Dedicated frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow), with Spark for data preparation

In practice, Spark's biggest role in ML is feature engineering at scale: the joins, windows and aggregations of Chapters 5–8 that turn billions of events into one row per customer.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 16 · Deep dive

Data leakage: fit transformers on the training set only

Wrong Right
scaler.fit(all_data) then split split, then pipeline.fit(train)
Encode categories seen only in the test set StringIndexer(handleInvalid="keep") for unseen values at scoring time
Features computed with future information (e.g. "total orders" including after the churn date) Compute features only from data before the prediction date

Leakage makes offline metrics look excellent and production results disappointing. A Pipeline fitted on the training split prevents the first two mistakes; the third is a modelling discipline — window functions with a time cut-off help.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Concept

In MLlib, what does calling .fit(df) on an Estimator return?

B. Estimators learn from data and return a fitted Model; the model's transform() adds prediction columns.

Chapter 16 · MCQ

Concept

Why does a model need VectorAssembler?

B. Every MLlib algorithm reads one features column of vector type.

Chapter 16 · MCQ

Concept

A StandardScaler was fitted on the full dataset before splitting into train and test. What is the problem?

B. Fit every transformer on the training data only — a Pipeline fitted on train does this automatically.

Predict the output

What does this print?

B. With 3 categories and dropLast=True (the default), the one-hot vector has 3 − 1 = 2 positions.

Chapter 16 · MCQ

Concept

A CrossValidator has a grid of 4 parameter combinations and numFolds=5. How many models does it train before refitting the best one?

D. Each of the 4 combinations is trained on each of the 5 folds: 20 fits, then one final fit of the best.

Satyaki Das — Assistant Professor, Rishihood University x Newton School of TechnologyGitHubLinkedInPySpark 4.2

Chapter 16 · MCQ

Debug the code

Scoring fails on new data with an "unseen label" error from StringIndexer. What is the fix?

B. handleInvalid="keep" maps categories not seen during fit to an extra index instead of failing.

Chapter 16 · MCQ

Concept

Which metric is 0.5 for random guessing and 1.0 for a perfect ranking of positives above negatives?

C. AUC measures ranking quality; random scores give 0.5.

SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY

SQL PySpark
SELECT a, b * 2 AS c df.select("a", (F.col("b") * 2).alias("c"))
WHERE x > 5 AND y = 'A' df.filter((F.col("x") > 5) & (F.col("y") == "A"))
WHERE z IS NULL df.filter(F.col("z").isNull())
WHERE c IN (1, 2) df.filter(F.col("c").isin(1, 2))
WHERE n LIKE 'A%' df.filter(F.col("n").like("A%"))
SELECT DISTINCT a df.select("a").distinct()
ORDER BY a DESC NULLS LAST df.orderBy(F.col("a").desc_nulls_last())
LIMIT 10 df.limit(10)
CASE WHEN … THEN … ELSE … END F.when(cond, v).when(…).otherwise(d)
COALESCE(a, b) F.coalesce("a", "b")
CAST(a AS INT) F.col("a").cast("int") (try_cast to avoid errors)

GROUP BY, joins, set operations

SQL PySpark
GROUP BY a + SUM(b) df.groupBy("a").agg(F.sum("b").alias("s"))

COUNT(DISTINCT b) F.countDistinct("b")
SUM(CASE WHEN c THEN x END) F.sum(F.when(c, F.col("x")))
INNER / LEFT / FULL JOIN … USING (k) a.join(b, "k", "inner" / "left" / "full")
WHERE EXISTS (…) a.join(b, "k", "left_semi")
WHERE NOT EXISTS (…) a.join(b, "k", "left_anti")

Window functions

SQL PySpark
OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY o) w = Window.partitionBy("p").orderBy("o")
ROW_NUMBER() / RANK() / DENSE_RANK() F.row_number().over(w) · F.rank() · F.dense_rank()
LAG(x) / LEAD(x) F.lag("x").over(w) · F.lead("x").over(w)
Running total F.sum("x").over(w.rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, 0))
Last 3 rows w.rowsBetween(-2, 0)
Last 7 days order by ts.cast("long"), rangeBetween(-7 * 86400, 0)
Top N per group withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("rn <= N")

Chapter 17 · Class notes

Performance checklist

Check How
How many shuffles? Count Exchange in df.explain()
Is the small table broadcast? Look for BroadcastHashJoin; else F.broadcast(small)
Are filters pushed down? PushedFilters / PartitionFilters in the scan
Is a task much slower than the rest? Spark UI stage page → skew → salt / AQE
Too many tiny files or tasks? AQE on; coalesce(n) before writing
Python UDF in a hot path? Replace with built-ins or a pandas UDF
Result reused several times? cache() … unpersist()
